definition.text: An equation that links one or more unknown functions to their derivatives, that is, to their rates of change.

facts.text: Such relations are common in scientific models, so differential equations are prominent in engineering, physics, economics and biology.
Only the simplest can be solved by explicit formulas, but many properties of the solutions can be found without solving them exactly.
When no formula exists, solutions can be approximated numerically on computers.
The theory of dynamical systems studies qualitative features of the solutions, such as their average long-run behaviour.
They arose with the invention of calculus by Isaac Newton and Gottfried Leibniz; Newton listed three kinds in a 1671 work.
They are used to model almost every physical, technical or biological process, from celestial motion to bridge design to neurons.
Complex adaptive systems may have so many elements that a system of differential equations becomes impractical and stops helping understanding.

definition.text: The main ways differential equations are classified: ordinary or partial, linear or nonlinear, homogeneous or not, and by order.

facts.text: An ordinary differential equation has an unknown function of one variable; a partial differential equation has unknown functions of several variables and their partial derivatives.
Linear differential equations have a well-developed theory, while few nonlinear ones can be solved exactly and they can behave chaotically over long times.
The order is the highest derivative that appears; equations describing nature usually have only first and second derivatives.
The class of an equation helps guide the choice of solution method.

definition.text: Extra information, such as a system's starting values, needed to pin down which of a differential equation's many solutions applies.

facts.text: The general solution of an nth-order ordinary differential equation contains n undetermined constants.
For a moving particle, the initial conditions are usually its position and velocity at the starting time.

definition.text: An equation in which time or another variable takes only separate values, relating a quantity's value at one point to its values at nearby points.

facts.text: Difference equations, also called recurrence relations, are the discrete-time counterpart of differential equations.
Numerical methods such as the Euler method approximate a differential equation by a matching difference equation.
Economists can model a price adjusting to excess demand either as a difference equation or, in continuous time, as a differential equation.
The Beverton–Holt population model is a discrete-time analogue of Verhulst's continuous-time logistic growth equation.

definition.text: Two alternative ways of modelling variables that change over time: as values in separate periods, or as values at every instant.

facts.text: Discrete time treats a variable as fixed within each period and jumping between periods, like a digital clock jumping from 10:37 to 10:38.
Continuous time lets time range over the real numbers, so there are infinitely many moments between any two points in time.
Economic activity happens continuously but can only be measured in steps, so GDP data come as a series of quarterly values.
Discrete time suits empirical work and time series models, while continuous-time theoretical models are often easier to handle mathematically.
Discrete time uses difference equations; continuous time uses differential equations.
Total discounted utility from a stream of consumption is a sum in discrete time and an integral in continuous time.

definition.text: The principle that any optimization problem can be viewed from two sides, the original (primal) problem or a matching dual problem.

facts.text: If the primal is a minimization problem, the dual is a maximization problem, and vice versa.
Any feasible value of the primal minimization is at least as large as any feasible value of the dual, so each bounds the other.
The usual Lagrangian dual adds the constraints to the objective using non-negative Lagrange multipliers, which become the dual variables.
Each constraint in an optimization problem has a shadow price, or dual variable.
In microeconomics, minimizing the spending needed to reach a level of happiness is the dual of maximizing utility.
John von Neumann conjectured the duality theorem of linear programming, drawing on his game theory; Albert W. Tucker's group published the first rigorous proofs in 1948.

definition.text: The difference between the optimal values of a primal optimization problem and its dual.

facts.text: For minimization problems the gap is never negative.
Strong duality holds when the gap is zero; otherwise it is positive and only weak duality holds.
For convex problems the gap is zero when a constraint qualification such as Slater's condition holds.
